findings.title: join() can return without force-stopping flusher processes
findings.body: SpanFlusher.join sets stopped and then calls next_step.join with the full timeout. If that consumes the budget, remaining_time <= 0 and the loop breaks without process.terminate() for every flusher process. close() intentionally does not stop these processes (to avoid a Redis memory spike at the start of rebalance), so join is the only force-stop path. Arroyo calls join with a finite timeout on shutdown and rebalance, and the consumer process stays alive across rebalance, so an un-killed flusher keeps flushing shards this consumer no longer owns. Those segments race the new assignee and are produced again to the buffered-segments topic. The wait is also sequential, so one slow process can exhaust the deadline and skip terminate() for the rest. The previous single-process join always terminated after the wait. After signaling stop, join must terminate and reap every process even when the timeout is already spent.

findings.title: Restart overlaps two flushers on the same shards
findings.body: _ensure_processes_alive SIGKILLs a hung flusher and immediately calls _create_process_for_shards without joining the old process. Process.kill() only sends the signal and returns, so the old process can still be inside flush_segments, Kafka produce, or done_flush_segments while the replacement starts flushing the same shard list. Both then read and clear the same Redis segments and emit them to buffered-segments, duplicating downstream data, and they also race on the shared backpressure_since and healthy_since values. The old Process object is dropped without being reaped, so each restart leaks a zombie until the consumer exits. The replacement must be started only after the previous process has actually exited.

findings.title: Comma-joined shard metric tags break tag parsing
findings.body: shard_tag is a comma-joined list of every shard a process owns and is emitted as a metric tag on spans.buffer.flusher.produce (key shard) and spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce (key shards). DogStatsD, which sentry.utils.metrics uses, treats commas as tag separators, so a value like 0,1,2 is parsed as extra tags and the series is dropped or attributed to the wrong tags. With the new CLI default --flusher-processes 1, one process owns every assigned partition, so this is the default path whenever a consumer has more than one partition. The value is also unique per partition assignment, so rebalances create a high-cardinality series. wait_produce uses the key shards while produce uses shard, so the two timers cannot be correlated. Emit a bounded process index, or one tag per shard, and use the same key.

findings.title: Drift wait is a no-op, so the flusher test stays racy
findings.body: test_basic patches time.sleep to a no-op, then calls time.sleep(0.1) to give the flusher thread time to observe current_drift after it is set to 9000. That call is the patched no-op, so it does not wait. step.join() immediately sets stopped, which can exit the flusher before it flushes, and (msg,) = messages then fails intermittently. The new multi-process test only checks process counts and never asserts that shards split across flushers are actually produced once. Patch sentry.spans.consumers.process.flusher.time.sleep instead of time.sleep, and wait until a message is produced.
